newsitem.title: UK: Major says British beef safe, but EU ban to stand.
newsitem.headline: Major says British beef safe, but EU ban to stand.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major insisted on Thursday that British beef was safe to eat, but the European Union's agriculture commissioner said a global ban on the meat would stay in place.

EU Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler said new scientific evidence linking mad cow disease with its human counterpart, the brain-wasting Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD), made it more important than ever to keep the ban in place.

"What the British scientists have discovered shows how serious the crisis is," Fischler told a Paris news conference. "We must make sure all the measures which have been put in place are maintained, because now we have to face the fact that the disease can be transmitted to people."
But Major said Britain had been operating on this assumption since March, and controls aimed at keeping potentially infectious beef out of the food supply were enough to protect human health.

"There's no new fresh public health concern. People can eat beef as safely today as they could yesterday, and I think it's perfectly safe," Major told BBC television. "There is no need for the European Union to panic and change its views."

Government scientific advisers agreed. "All the necessary restrictions on (infected) British beef going into the human food chain are now in place," John Pattison, senior scientific adviser on Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE or mad cow disease), told BBC radio.
Britain's top experts on BSE and CJD reported on Wednesday they had found a chemical signature that showed marked similarities between a new variant of CJD and mad cow disease.
The new variant was formally identified in March after 10 Britons succumbed to it and researchers said the most likely cause was eating BSE-infected beef.
The EU immediately slapped the ban on British beef -- a heavy blow after the British meat industry's decade-long battle with the BSE epidemic.
The news caused beef sales in Britain to fall to just over 70 percent of normal, but they have now recovered to 85 percent.
Delegates to the Meat and Livestock Commission's Festival of British Beef in London were sanguine on Thursday.

"The safeguards that have been put in place were based on a worst case assumption that there could be a link between BSE and CJD. These safeguards are working extremely effectively," Don Curry, chairman of the commission, told the conference.
"The new research doesn't worry me at all," said Helen Kent, a caterer for Kent County police and public schools.
"The whole thing has been exaggerated," she added as she tucked into a plate of stir-fried beef.
"I think that if there has been a problem, it has been an historic one," agreed John Gray, a caterer in Cambridgeshire.

Jane Jones, a caterer in Shropshire, said such statements made her feel a little safer. But she admitted she had avoided beef since March and was pointedly eating quiche instead of the many meat dishes on offer.
